items.title: 3.6 Law of conservation of angular momentum

blocks.title: Law of conservation of angular momentum
blocks.text: If no external torque acts on a system, the total angular momentum of the system remains constant: L_total = L1 + L2 + ... = constant.

The law of conservation of angular momentum is one of the fundamental principles of physics; it has been verified from the cosmological to the sub-microscopic level. Its effect is readily apparent when a single isolated spinning body alters its moment of inertia: if a body of moment of inertia I1 spinning with angular speed omega1 alters its moment of inertia to I2, its angular speed omega2 also changes so that its angular momentum remains constant, hence I1 omega1 = I2 omega2. The angular momentum is a vector quantity with direction along the axis of rotation, so the direction of angular momentum along the axis also remains fixed: the axis of rotation of an object will not change its orientation unless an external torque causes it to do so. This fact is of great importance for the Earth as it moves around the Sun: no other sizeable torque is experienced by the Earth, because the major force acting on it is the pull of the Sun, so the Earth's axis of rotation remains fixed in one direction with reference to the universe around us.
Examples of conservation of angular momentum
A man diving from a diving board

A diver jumping from a springboard has to take a few somersaults in the air before touching the water (Fig. 3.18). After leaving the springboard he curls his body by rolling his arms and legs in; his moment of inertia decreases and he spins in mid-air with a large angular velocity. When about to touch the water he stretches out his arms and legs, enters the water at a gentle speed and gets a smooth dive.

blocks.alt: A sequence of positions of one diver: walking along the board, raising a knee, taking off stretched out with the arms up, then curled up in three somersault positions with gold arrows showing the spin, and finally stretched out head first for the entry into the water.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.18: A man diving from a diving board (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.18).
blocks.long_description: The book prints this figure as a photo-sequence; it is redrawn here as a sketch.

blocks.text: An ice skater can increase his angular velocity by folding his arms and bringing the stretched leg close to the other leg; by doing so he decreases his moment of inertia, so the angular speed increases. When he stretches his hands and a leg outward, the moment of inertia increases and the angular velocity decreases: angular momentum = (moment of inertia)(angular velocity), L = I x omega.

blocks.alt: Two front views of a skater. Left, labelled I - large, omega - small: arms stretched out sideways, with a wide red ring round the arms and a small one round the feet. Right, labelled I - small, omega - large: arms folded across the chest and legs together, with small red rings round the body from chest to feet. Below: Angular momentum = (Moment of inertia) (Angular velocity), L = I x omega.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.19: An ice skater using angular momentum (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.19).

blocks.text: A person holding some weight in his hands standing on a turntable

A person stands on a turntable with heavy masses (dumb-bells) in his outstretched hands; as he draws his hands inward his angular speed at once increases, because the moment of inertia decreases on drawing the hands inwards, which increases the angular speed.

blocks.alt: Two sketches of a man standing on a turntable with a dumb-bell in each hand. (a) Arms stretched out sideways, with a dashed circle round the path of the hands. (b) Arms drawn in, the dumb-bells close to his sides. A small curled arrow above each head shows the rotation.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.20: Man with masses in his hands on a turntable; conservation of angular momentum requires that as the man pulls his arms in, the angular velocity increases (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.20).
blocks.long_description: The book prints this figure as two photographs; it is redrawn here as a sketch.

blocks.text: A mechanical device consisting of a heavy wheel with an axle, used to store rotational energy, smooth out output fluctuations and provide stability in a wide range of applications such as bicycles and other vehicles, industrial machinery, gyroscopes, ships and spacecraft. When a flywheel spins, its angular momentum resists changes to its orientation, maintaining stability, which is useful in systems that need precise control over their orientation without external interference. The flywheel called the balance wheel regulates the time-keeping mechanism in mechanical clocks and watches by maintaining a controlled rate of oscillation (Do You Know).

blocks.alt: A heavy disc with a thick dark rim and a blue face with a central hub and bolt holes, mounted on an axle that sticks out to the left through a small blue collar.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.21: A flywheel (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.21).
blocks.long_description: The book prints this figure as a photograph; it is redrawn here as a sketch.

blocks.text: A device used to maintain its orientation relative to the Earth's axis, or to resist changes in its orientation. It consists of a mounted flywheel pivoted in supporting rings and works on the law of conservation of angular momentum due to its large moment of inertia. Spinning at a large angular speed it gains a large angular momentum, so it is difficult to change the orientation of its rotational axis: a change in orientation requires a change in angular momentum, and to change the direction of a large angular momentum a correspondingly large torque is required. Even if the gyroscope is tilted it keeps levitated without falling. The main applications of the gyroscope are in the guiding systems of aeroplanes, submarines and space vehicles, to maintain a specific direction in space and keep a steady course.

blocks.alt: A gyroscope on a stand: a heavy rotor on a horizontal axle, mounted in an inner ring, a horizontal ring and an outer ring held by the stand. A red arrow along the axle to the left is labelled L = I omega and Angular momentum. On the right a curled arrow round the axle end is labelled Spin axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.22: The gyroscope (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.22).
